exp.1:23:
It says that what the believers heard from the beginning, that is, the gospel message about Jesus, must remain firm in them. Staying put means it does not leave or depart. If that message stays alive in them, they will also remain united with the Son and the Father.

The apostle John speaks here, traditionally recognized as the author of this letter. He writes to believers who faced teachers denying that Jesus is the Christ. John wants to protect them from deception by reminding them of the original teaching they received.

For today: return often to the basics of your faith. Read the Gospels, review who Jesus is, and compare what you hear in social media, sermons, or conversations against that. Whatever departs from the original message, test with care.
exp.0:1:
The explanation says that the eternal life, which is Jesus Christ, became visible. The words "was manifested" and "has appeared to us" mean that he let himself be seen clearly. The apostles saw him, bear witness to him, and announce him to others. That life was "with the Father," that is, it existed alongside God before coming into the world.

The speaker is the apostle John, according to Christian tradition, together with other witnesses. He writes to believers to affirm that Jesus was real, that he could be seen and touched. He does this to strengthen their faith and their union with God and with one another. The verse is in parentheses because it interrupts the sentence to explain what came before.

Our faith does not rest on ideas, but on a real person who made himself known. Today you can share with others what Christ has done in you, simply and sincerely, like a witness who tells what he knows.
exp.1:0:
John speaks to them with affection, like a father to his children. He writes so that they will not sin. But if anyone does sin, they are not left without hope: we have an advocate (someone who defends us and speaks on our behalf) before the Father, Jesus Christ, the righteous one.

The one speaking is John, the apostle, already elderly, according to Christian tradition. He writes to believers and shows them two things: God calls them to live without sin, and also offers forgiveness. The following verses explain that Jesus is the atoning sacrifice, that is, the sacrifice that reconciles us to God.

For today: do not use grace as an excuse to sin, but do not turn away from God out of shame when you fail. Acknowledge your error, ask for forgiveness, and remember that Jesus defends you. His righteousness, not your perfection, gives you confidence to return to God.
exp.1:15:
It says that everything that rules in the world without God comes down to three things: the disordered desires of the body (the lust of the flesh), the desire to have everything the eyes take in (the lust of the eyes), and pride in what a person owns or achieves in this life (the pride of life). John affirms that these things do not come from the Father, but from the world.

The author, traditionally the apostle John, writes to believers like a pastor writing to his "little children." He encourages them because they have come to know God, and at the same time warns them not to let love for the world take the place of love for the Father. "World" here does not mean creation, but the system that lives with its back turned to God.

Today we can ask ourselves what desire, what image, or what craving to look good is taking hold of our hearts. Surrendering it to God in prayer and seeking his will helps us love what endures.
exp.2:19:
For if our heart condemns us, God is greater than our heart and knows all things. "Condemns" here means "accuses" or "condemns." That is, God is not limited by our feelings or by our doubts.

The apostle John writes to believers he calls "little children." He has just asked them for a love that shows itself in deeds, not only in words. Now he comforts them: when we truly love but still feel guilty or insecure, we can rest in God. Interpreters explain this verse in several ways, but almost all agree that John seeks to give them assurance.

For today: when guilt or doubt speak loudly to you, do not stay alone with what you feel. Pray, confess whatever is necessary, rest in the knowledge that God knows you completely, and keep loving with concrete deeds.
exp.1:18:
They went out from the fellowship of believers, but they never truly belonged to it in their hearts. The explanation says "sure" means "without doubt," and "stayed" means they would have remained. Their leaving made it clear that not everyone who moves among believers is truly of Christ.

The apostle John, now an old man, speaks to Christians whom he calls "little children." There are false teachers, called "antichrists," who denied truths about Jesus and left the church. John wants the faithful not to be troubled or to doubt their faith. Some believe this refers to an actual division in the churches of Asia Minor, though the text gives no further details.

For today: if someone walks away from the church or from the faith, do not let that shake your confidence in Christ. Examine your own heart, remain in the truth, and pray with love for those who have gone.
exp.1:1:
He says that Jesus is the "propitiation" for our sins. This word means the sacrifice that satisfies God's justice and removes guilt, making forgiveness possible. And he adds that this is not only for the believers he is writing to ("for ours only"), but also "for the sins of the whole world." Christians understand the reach of this phrase in different ways, but all agree that the offer of forgiveness is wide.

Here the apostle John speaks as an older pastor who calls his readers "my little children." He writes so that they will not sin, but he reminds them that if anyone falls, they have an "advocate" before the Father: Jesus. Then John says that knowing God is shown by obeying him.

For today: if you fail, do not run from God or sink into guilt. Come to Jesus with sincerity, trust his forgiveness, and walk again in obedience.
exp.0:8:
This verse says that if we honestly recognize and tell God what we have done wrong, he responds with faithfulness and justice: he forgives us and cleanses us from all unrighteousness. To "confess" means to agree with God about our sin, without hiding it or excusing it. "Unrighteousness" is everything that is crooked or outside of what is right.

The speaker is John, an apostle of Jesus, now an older man, writing to believers. Before this, he says that no one can claim to have no sin without deceiving themselves. Then he adds that denying it makes God a liar. John does not intend to frighten anyone, but to show that there is a sure forgiveness through the blood of Jesus.

For today: when you fail, do not hide or make excuses for yourself. Speak with God openly, name what you did, and trust that he keeps his promise. If you have hurt someone, also seek to ask that person for forgiveness.
exp.2:9:
This verse says that you can recognize who are children of God and who are children of the devil by the way they live. Whoever does not practice righteousness, that is, what is right and good before God, and does not love his brother, does not belong to God.

Here the apostle John, traditionally identified as the author of this letter, speaks. He writes to believers to help them tell true faith apart from false teachings. For him, faith shows itself in a life that resembles Christ. Some scholars debate how to understand the phrase about not practicing sin, but the general meaning is that the believer does not live by practicing sin.

Today we can ask ourselves: how do I treat my brothers and sisters in faith and the people around me? This week, take one concrete step of love: forgive, help, or visit someone.
exp.1:24:
This verse says that God's great promise to us is eternal life. "He" refers to Jesus, the Son. Eternal life is not only living forever, but a life of relationship with God that begins now and continues without end.

John, one of the leaders of the early church, writes to Christians who were facing false teachers. These teachers denied who Jesus is. John asks them to remain in what they heard from the beginning, the message about Christ, and reminds them that remaining in the Son joins them to the Father and assures them of this promise.

For today: when you doubt or feel confused by so many voices, return to the basics of your faith in Jesus. Read the Gospels often and remember that your hope rests on a promise from God, not on your own strength.
exp.1:16:
This verse says that the world and everything people desire in it are passing away; they come to an end. "Lust" is a strong, disordered desire that takes control of us. By contrast, whoever does the will of God, that is, whoever lives as pleases Him, remains forever.

The apostle John, an elderly pastor, speaks to believers whom he calls "little children." He warns them not to set their hearts on what opposes the Father: the desires of the flesh, the desires of the eyes, and the pride of life. Then he speaks of false teachers who have left the community. In this way he reminds them where what truly lasts is found.

For today: before pursuing something you desire, ask yourself whether it will last or whether it is only passing. Today, choose one small act of obedience to God, such as forgiving, being honest, or setting aside time to pray. That has eternal value.
exp.2:12:
John tells the believers not to be surprised or thrown off if the world rejects them or treats them with hostility. The words "marvel" and "wonder" in the verse above mean being amazed or taken aback. John calls them "my brothers" with affection.

John the apostle is writing to believers who faced rejection. He has just spoken of Cain, who killed his brother because his brother's works were righteous and his own were evil. In this way, John shows that the rejection of the righteous is not new. He then contrasts that hatred with love between brothers, which is a sign of new life.

Today, if people criticize you or leave you out because you live as Jesus did, do not assume that something is wrong with you or with your faith. Instead of responding with bitterness, seek to love your brothers and sisters in the faith and those who reject you, and rest in the knowledge that God sustains you.
exp.2:10:
This verse says that the central message believers have heard since they came to know Jesus is simple: we should love one another. "From the beginning" means from the start of their Christian life, when they received the teaching of Christ.

The speaker is the apostle John, according to Christian tradition, and he writes to believers like a shepherd who cares for them. Shortly before, he has said that the children of God are recognized because they practice righteousness and love their brother. Right after, he gives Cain, who killed his brother, as the opposite example.

For today: think of a person close to you, from your family or your church, with whom you have some tension. Today, do something concrete for them: pray for their good, offer them help, or take the first step toward reconciliation.
exp.4:11:
This verse says that eternal life is connected to a person: Jesus, the Son of God. "Having the Son" means receiving him, believing in him, and being joined to him. Whoever has him has the life God gives. Whoever does not have him does not have that life. Here "life" refers to eternal life, a life with God that begins now and does not end.

The writer is John, one of Jesus' earliest followers, according to Christian tradition. He writes to believers who faced doubts and false teachings. Just before this verse, he explains that God himself gave testimony about his Son. Then he states his purpose: that believers may know with certainty that they have eternal life.

Today, instead of looking for security in your efforts or achievements, rest in Jesus. Each day you can speak to him, read about him, and trust his promise. Your peace does not depend on how much you do, but on who you have.
exp.1:4:
The explanation says that whoever keeps God's word shows that the love of God has reached its goal in him. "Charity" is an old word for love. "Perfected" here means complete and mature, not that the person never fails. Obedience is the sign that we truly remain united with God, that we are in him.

The apostle John, according to Christian tradition, writes to believers who are already mature and to others confused by teachers who claimed to know God without living as he teaches. Earlier, John said that whoever claims to know God and does not obey is a liar. Here he gives the other side: obedience confirms a real faith. Some understand "the love of God" as the love God has for us, and others as our love toward him; both meanings fit.

For today: instead of only asking yourself "what do I feel toward God?", ask "what step of obedience can I take today?" Perhaps forgiving, being honest, or helping someone.
exp.3:9:
This verse says that true love does not begin with us but with God. We did not love him first; he loved us and sent his Son as the sacrifice that takes away guilt and restores the broken relationship with God, because of our sins.

The apostle John, according to Christian tradition, writes to believers to encourage them to live in love. Earlier he explained that God is love and that he sent his Son to give us life. Then he concludes that, if God loved us in this way, we ought to love one another. Some scholars believe he is also correcting false teachings of his time.

For today: when it is hard for you to love someone, remember that God loved you without your deserving it. That gratitude can help you forgive, take the first step, and treat with kindness the person who has not earned it.
exp.3:0:
John writes to believers and calls them "beloved." He tells them not to believe every spiritual message, but to test it to see whether it comes from God. To test means to examine something carefully. His point that false prophets have already gone out into the world means they have already appeared. There are many false prophets, that is, people who speak in God's name without being sent by him.

The one speaking is the apostle John, according to Christian tradition, writing to churches that were facing deceptive teachings. The verses that follow give the main test: recognizing that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, that is, that God truly became a human being. John wants to protect the community from ideas that denied this truth.

Today, before we accept what we hear in a sermon, on social media, or from friends, let us compare it with the Bible and with what it says about Jesus. Being simple does not mean being naive: examining things with humility and prayer is a way of loving the truth.
exp.4:13:
This verse says that believers have confidence before God: if we ask him for something that agrees with what he wills, he hears us. Some older wording needs a note: where the text uses an archaic word for "ask," it means simply "ask," and the phrase about what agrees with his will means "in line with what he desires." Where it says he hears us, this means he attends to us and receives us with favor.

The author is John, writing to believers. In the verse before, he tells them he wrote so they would know they have eternal life. Now he moves from that assurance to assurance in prayer. He then speaks of praying for a brother who sins. About the "sin that leads to death," interpreters do not agree on its exact meaning.

For today: when you pray, do not only present your wishes. Ask God to teach you what pleases him, read it in his Word, and pray with confidence, knowing that your Father hears you.
exp.1:3:
This verse says that if someone claims to know God but does not obey what He commands, they are lying. Their life contradicts their words. "Keeping his commandments" means carrying them out and living according to them. The phrase "the one who" in the verse refers to "that person."

The apostle John writes to believers to give them assurance and to warn them against false teachings. Just before this, he speaks of the forgiveness Christ gives us. Here he makes clear that knowing God is not just an idea or a statement, but a relationship that shows itself in obedience. John is not speaking of being perfect, since he has already said that Jesus forgives our sins, but of the direction of a life.

For today: check whether your way of living supports what you say you believe. Choose one command of Jesus, such as forgiving or loving someone difficult, and practice it this week, asking God for help.
exp.4:2:
This verse says that loving God does not stay in words or feelings: it is shown by obeying him. It also says that his commandments "are not grievous," that is, they are not a heavy burden or hard to carry.

The one speaking is the apostle John, according to Christian tradition, writing to believers. Earlier he spoke of loving the children of God, and afterward he says that faith overcomes the world. For John, love, obedience and faith go together. Obeying is not a burden, because whoever has been born of God receives a new life that desires to please him.

Today, when a decision costs you something, such as forgiving or being honest, do not see it as a burden. Make it a response of love to God, and ask him for help to carry it out.
exp.2:20:
It says that if our conscience does not accuse us or condemn us, we can approach God with assurance and without fear. The word "beloved" in the verse means "dear ones" or "those we love." The word that rebukes us means to accuse us or make us feel guilty. Confidence is the freedom to speak to God without fear.

John the apostle writes to believers whom he calls his beloved. Earlier he told them that when our heart accuses us, God is greater than our heart and knows all things. Now he speaks of the opposite case: when we live in love and obedience, our conscience is at peace and we can pray with confidence. Some scholars debate how these two verses relate, but the central idea is assurance before God.

Today, if you feel guilty, bring it to God honestly and remember that He is greater than your guilt. And when your conscience is at peace, pray with confidence, without doubting that He hears you.
exp.4:1:
It says that we know we truly love the other believers, the children of God, when we love God and keep his commandments. The word "keep" here means to obey and carry out.

The apostle John, traditionally identified as the author, wrote this to Christians who needed assurance in their faith. He has just said that whoever loves the Father also loves his children. Now he ties together love for God, love for brothers and sisters, and obedience as signs that go together. Then he clarifies that his commandments are not burdensome.

For today: if you find it hard to love someone in your church, don't start by forcing feelings. First draw near to God in prayer and obedience, and ask him to love that person through you. Then take one concrete step of kindness this week.
exp.4:10:
It says that the central message God gives is this: he has given us eternal life, and that life is not separate from Jesus, but is found in his Son. The word "testimony" means a firm declaration of something that is true. Here, God himself is the one who bears witness.

The author is John, who writes to believers to strengthen their assurance. There was confusion and voices teaching different things about Jesus. For this reason John reminds them that God's testimony is worth more than any human word. At the end of this passage he explains his purpose: that they may know they have eternal life.

For today: if you have trusted in Jesus, you can rest in the fact that eternal life is a gift and not a prize you earn. When you doubt, do not look at your mistakes or your feelings, but at what God has already said about his Son.
exp.2:21:
It says that God grants what we ask when we live in obedience to Him and seek to please Him. "Whatever" is not a license to ask for whatever we want; it speaks of a life lined up with God. "Dear friends" is the word for those we love.

The one speaking is John, an elderly apostle, who writes to believers to give them assurance. Earlier he speaks of the heart that accuses us and of confidence before God. Then he explains that His command is to believe in Jesus and to love one another. In this way, "keeping his commandments" centers on faith and love. Some understand that prayer is heard because our desires increasingly resemble God's.

Today, before you pray, you might ask yourself: "Does what I'm asking reflect love and trust in Jesus?" Pray with sincerity, and if your conscience accuses you, remember that God is greater than your heart.
exp.0:6:
It says that if we live in the light, that is, in the truth and holiness of God, just as he is light, we have fellowship and unity with one another. Furthermore, the blood of Jesus, his Son, cleanses us from all sin. The verse's wording "But if" introduces this contrast, and "walk" refers to the way we live each day.

The writer is John, one of the apostles according to Christian tradition, although the letter does not name him. He writes to believers to encourage them to live in the truth. Earlier he said that God is light, and that we cannot claim to be close to him while we live in the darkness of sin and deceit.

For today: there is no need to pretend we are perfect. We can live honestly before God and others, admit our failures, and trust that Jesus cleanses us. That honesty also strengthens friendship among brothers and sisters in the faith.
exp.1:10:
This verse says that whoever holds hatred against his brother lives in spiritual darkness. He is not only in the dark, but walks in it without knowing where he is going, because that darkness has blinded him. "Hate" here means to despise or reject with bitterness. "Brother" here refers above all to the brother in the faith, although some extend it to every neighbor.

The one speaking is John, the apostle, now an old man, and he writes to believers with affection, calling them "little children." He wants them to be sure that they know God, and so he shows that love for one's brothers and sisters is a clear sign of living in the light of Christ.

For today: if you carry resentment against someone, bring it honestly before God. Ask Him to help you forgive, and take a concrete step, such as praying for that person or seeking reconciliation.
exp.2:7:
It says that whoever makes sin their practice and habit is like the devil, who has sinned from the beginning. "Whoever commits sin" does not speak of a single fall, but of living in sin without repenting. It also says that Jesus, the Son of God, came to undo, that is, to destroy and disarm, what the devil has done.

John the apostle writes to believers whom he calls "little children." There are false teachers who are confusing them, and he tells them that true faith shows itself in a life of righteousness and love. Some understand "does not sin" as a constant practice, not as absolute perfection.

For today: if Christ came to undo the works of the devil, do not make peace with a sin that keeps repeating. Confess it to God, ask for his help, and seek support from trustworthy brothers and sisters.
exp.4:15:
It says that if anyone sees a brother in the faith committing a sin that is not deadly, he should ask God for him, and God will give him life. It also says there is a deadly sin, and that for this one John does not tell us to pray. "Ask" means to request; the old word "see" is the same as "look at."

John the apostle writes to believers to give them assurance. He has just said that God hears prayers made according to his will. Now he applies that to praying for others. It is not clear what the "sin unto death" is; some think of persistently rejecting Christ, others of a sin that brings physical death. The Bible does not fully clarify it.

For today: when you see a brother fall, do not criticize or ignore him; pray for him with confidence and humility. Leave to God what you do not understand.
exp.2:1:
This verse says that believers are already children of God, though it is not yet fully clear what we will be. John promises that when Christ appears, we will be like him, because we will see him as he is.

Here the apostle John speaks as a pastor writing to believers. He reminds them of the Father's love, who calls us children, even though the world does not understand us, because it did not know Jesus either. Then he connects this hope with a pure life, as the next verse shows. Christians understand in different ways how this transformation will happen, but they all agree that God will complete it.

Today you can rest in your identity as a child of God, even when you feel incomplete. That hope encourages you to pursue a pure life and to trust that God will finish his work in you.
exp.1:5:
This verse says that whoever claims to remain united with Jesus should live the way Jesus lived. To remain in him means to stay in fellowship with Christ. To walk is an older way of speaking of daily conduct: how we think, how we treat others, and how we make decisions.

John, traditionally regarded as the apostle, writes to believers to give them assurance and also to correct them. Some were saying they knew God, but their lives did not show it. Earlier, John spoke of keeping the commandments; later, he will speak of love and of light. Here he joins faith with conduct.

For today: it is not enough to say "I believe." Think of a situation from this week, such as an argument or a temptation, and ask yourself: "How would Jesus respond?" Ask God for help to act that way, with humility and love.
exp.1:8:
This verse says that someone can claim to live in the light, that is, in fellowship with God, but if they hate their brother, they are still in darkness. "Hate" means to despise or to treat someone with hostility and contempt. The words "still" and "even until now" stress that such a person has not truly come out of the darkness.

The apostle John writes to believers and reminds them of the command to love one another, which Jesus taught from the beginning. He calls it both old and new at once, because the light of Christ is already shining and makes that love visible. John wants his readers to test whether their faith is genuine, since speaking well is not enough.

Today we can ask ourselves whether there is someone we hold a grudge against, even if we go to church. Ask God to help you take one concrete step: pray for that person, forgive them, or seek reconciliation.
exp.2:3:
This verse says that whoever practices sin is also breaking God's law. John puts it directly: to sin is to transgress, that is, to step over what God has commanded. The phrase "commits sin" speaks of an ongoing practice, not an isolated fall. The word "transgresses" means to break or violate.

The speaker is the apostle John, writing to believers who are already children of God and who are waiting to see Christ. Just before this, he speaks of that hope, which moves us to purify ourselves. Then he reminds us that Jesus came to take away our sins. Many scholars think John was also correcting those who took sin lightly.

For today: let us not minimize sin or call it a "small mistake." Each day we can ask God to show us where we are disobeying him, confess it honestly, and trust that Christ forgives and strengthens us.
exp.3:18:
This verse says that our love for God is a response. First God loved us, and because of that we are able to love him. The word "á" is an old way of writing "a," and "le amamos" means "we love him."

The author is John, who writes to believers. Earlier he spoke of how God's love, when it matures in us, drives out fear of judgment. Then he uses this verse to show that loving God is seen in how we treat our brother. John says this with great firmness.

For today: when it is hard for you to love someone, remember how much God has loved you. Today, pray and take one concrete step of kindness toward that person, such as listening to them, forgiving them, or helping them.
exp.2:2:
He says that the one who has the hope of seeing Christ and being like him does not stay still, but purifies himself. "Whoever" means "every one who." "Purifies himself" means that he works to live free from sin. "Pure" shows that Jesus is the model of purity.

John the apostle writes to believers to encourage and warn them. He has just said that we are children of God and that, when Christ appears, we will be like him. Then he explains that sin goes against God's law and that Jesus came to take it away. Some scholars see the purifying as the believer's effort with God's help; the text does not say we do it alone.

For today: let the hope of seeing Jesus motivate you. Today, choose one attitude or habit that does not please God, and ask him for help to change it step by step.
exp.2:8:
Whoever has been born of God does not live in the practice of sin. The "seed" is the life or nature that God places in the believer, like a seed that bears fruit. The phrase "cannot sin" can be understood in two ways: that he cannot live in sin as a habit, or that his new nature resists it. "Commits sin" speaks of a constant practice.

John, the apostle, now elderly, writes to believers whom he calls "little children." He warns them against teachers who were deceiving them, saying that a person can live in sin and still be righteous. John shows that true faith is seen in a life of righteousness and love for one's brother.

Today, do not use grace as an excuse to keep doing wrong. If you have trusted in Christ, ask God to change your habits and practice love this week. If you fail, John himself says in 1:9 that God forgives the one who confesses.
exp.3:6:
The explanation says that believers should love one another, because love has its origin in God. The word for "beloved" in the verse does not appear in the verse you are reading, so the phrase used here is simply "beloved", which is in the verse. Where the explanation refers to "everyone who loves", that is the same as "every one that loveth". Whoever truly loves shows that they have been born of God and that they know God.

The apostle John, already elderly according to Christian tradition, writes to communities of believers. Earlier he spoke about distinguishing truth from error, since false teachings were circulating. Now he adds another sign: love. For John, sound doctrine and love go together. He then explains that God is love and that he showed this by sending his Son.

Today we can ask ourselves: who is hard for me to love in my church, my family, or my work? Ask God for help to take one concrete step this week: forgiving, listening with patience, or serving with a simple gesture, without expecting anything in return.
exp.0:2:
This verse says that the apostles declare what they saw and heard of Jesus. Their purpose is that the readers also may have fellowship with them, that is, a shared union and friendship. And that fellowship does not end with them: it is with God the Father and with his Son Jesus Christ.

The author, traditionally identified as the apostle John, writes as a direct witness of Jesus. He speaks of having seen, heard, and touched him. His letter seeks to strengthen believers who were facing false teachings about Christ, and so he insists that his message comes from a real experience. This prepares what follows: his joy and the message that God is light.

For today: the Christian faith is not just a personal idea, but a shared life. Look for a church or a group of believers where you can hear the Word, pray, and walk with others while you grow in your relationship with God.
exp.4:17:
We know that anyone born of God does not keep on sinning. The one who was begotten of God (in the view of many interpreters, Jesus Christ) keeps watch over him, and so the evil one, the devil, does not get a hold on him. He cannot dominate or permanently harm him.

Within the text, the word that appears here refers to himself, meaning the one who is cared for.

John, an elderly pastor, writes to believers who are unsure of themselves because of false teachers. He had been speaking about praying for a brother who sins. Now he states with confidence what we know: the new life in God changes the direction of the heart. There are several opinions about who the one begotten of God is and what the sin leading to death is; the text does not fully explain this.

For today: when you fall into temptation, do not give up or doubt your faith. Draw near to Christ, ask for his help, and trust that he protects you.
exp.0:0:
This verse says that the author is speaking of something real that existed from the beginning, and that he himself experienced it with his senses: he heard it, he saw it, he looked at it carefully, and his hands touched it. It refers to the Word of life, a title of Jesus Christ. The word "handled" means that they touched it with their hands.

The letter does not name its author. Christian tradition attributes it to the apostle John, although some scholars debate this. The writer presents himself as a direct witness of Jesus. His purpose is to give a firm testimony, as the following context shows, so that others may believe and share in fellowship with the Father and with the Son.

For today: our faith rests on a trustworthy testimony, not on vague ideas. You can give thanks for that testimony, read the Gospels with attention, and share with others what Jesus has done in your life, simply and sincerely.
exp.4:6:
The verse says that in heaven there are three who bear witness: the Father, the Word (that is, the Word, who is Jesus Christ), and the Holy Spirit. And it affirms that these three are one. It is one of the clearest expressions of the unity of God in three persons.

The apostle John writes to believers to give them assurance that Jesus is truly the Son of God. An important point: this phrase does not appear in the oldest Greek manuscripts, and many modern Bibles omit it or place it in a footnote. The King James Version does include it. Even so, the teaching of one God in three persons rests on other passages, such as Matthew 28:19.

If God himself testifies about his Son, you can trust that your faith rests on something firm. When you doubt, return to the Word and ask the Spirit to give you assurance.
exp.1:14:
John asks us not to set our hearts on the world or on the things in it. Here "world" does not refer to God's creation or to people, but to the system of desires and values that lives turned away from God. If someone loves the world in this way, John says, the love of the Father is not in that person. The two loves cannot fit together in the same heart.

The apostle John writes to believers at different stages of faith, having just reminded them that they know the Father and have overcome the evil one. For this reason he urges them not to be caught up in what is passing. He then explains that the world is passing away, but whoever does the will of God remains forever.

Today you might ask yourself: "What takes up more of my heart: money, appearance, success, or God?" Ask the Lord to order your desires, and set aside time each day for his Word.
exp.2:13:
It says that Christians can have assurance that we are no longer spiritually dead, but alive in God. The sign is that we love the brethren, that is, other believers. Whoever does not love his brother remains in spiritual death. Here the word "hate" in the verse refers to a rejection of the heart, not just a passing feeling.

John, the apostle, writes to believers who face the rejection of the world. Earlier he reminded them of Cain, who killed his brother out of envy. Now he contrasts that hatred with the love that comes from God. John does not say that love saves us, but shows that we have already received new life.

For today: think of someone in your church or family with whom you have resentment. Ask God to help you take a concrete step of love toward them: a phone call, an apology, a practical help, or a sincere prayer for that person.
exp.4:16:
It says that all unrighteousness is sin, and that none of it is small before God. But it also makes clear that not every sin is "unto death." "Unrighteousness" here means whatever is not right; "sin unto death" is a sin so serious that it leads to separation from God.

John the apostle writes to believers to give them assurance and to guide them in prayer. He has just asked them to pray for a brother who sins. What exactly the "sin unto death" is, is not explained here, and scholars understand it in several ways. Many relate it to persistently rejecting Christ.

For today: if you see a brother fall, do not judge him harshly or ignore him. Pray for him with hope, trusting that God forgives and gives life to whoever turns back to Him.
exp.4:4:
This verse asks a question in order to give a clear answer: only the one who believes that Jesus is the Son of God overcomes the world. To overcome means to come out victorious, and "the world" here is not the creation, but the system of ideas and desires that stands against God.

John, already an old man, writes to Christians who faced false teachers who denied who Jesus was. Earlier he spoke of obeying God out of love, and said that our faith is the victory. Here he clarifies that this faith has a specific center: Jesus, the Son of God. Some scholars point out that the final part of the wider passage, about the three in heaven, is missing from the oldest Greek manuscripts.

For today: when you feel pressure to live like everyone else, or fear overtakes you, return to the basics. Trust in Jesus again and ask him for help. Your victory does not depend on your own strength, but on whom you believe.
exp.3:20:
This verse says that God gave us a clear command: whoever loves God must also love his brother. In the old text, the word for "to" appears only as a spelling variant of the ordinary form, and "brother" refers above all to a fellow believer, although many understand that the principle reaches every neighbor.

The writer is John, traditionally identified as the apostle, though the letter does not give his name. He writes to believers so that they may live in truth and love. Shortly before, he says that our love comes from the love of God, and that saying "I love God" while hating one's brother is a contradiction. "He" in this verse refers to God or to Christ.

For today: if you say you love God, look at how you treat those who are close to you. This week, take one concrete step: ask forgiveness, help someone, or pray for a person with whom you have tension.
exp.4:5:
The verse says that Jesus Christ came by water and blood, and not by water only, but by water and blood. Moreover, the Spirit bears witness to this, because the Spirit is the truth. The word "witness" here means to affirm or confirm that something is true.

The author is John, writing to believers who faced false teachers. Some of them denied that Jesus was truly God become man. Many understand the "water" as his baptism and the "blood" as his death on the cross, affirming that Jesus fulfilled his entire mission. Scholars do not fully agree on the exact meaning of the "water," but John's emphasis is clear: Jesus is real, and his work is complete.

Today we can rest in the fact that our faith does not rest on vague ideas, but on a real person who lived, died, and triumphed for us. When you doubt, remember that the Spirit confirms that truth in your heart.
exp.1:22:
This verse says that the Son and the Father cannot be separated. Whoever rejects or denies Jesus does not have a true relationship with God the Father either. But whoever openly acknowledges Jesus as the Son of God also has the Father. "Confess" here means to declare and acknowledge Jesus publicly, not merely to think it.

The author is John, who writes like a loving shepherd to believers who already know the truth. He writes because teachers had appeared who denied that Jesus is the Christ. John wants believers not to be confused and to remain steadfast in what they heard from the beginning.

Today we can live this out by confessing Jesus simply, at home, at work, or with friends, without being ashamed. And if someone says they love God but sets Jesus aside, we can answer them with kindness and rely on what the Bible says.
exp.4:12:
This verse says that John wrote this letter to those who already believe in Jesus, the Son of God. His purpose is that they may know with certainty that they have eternal life.

The speaker is John, the apostle, according to the oldest Christian tradition. He writes to believers who faced doubts and false teachings. Just before this, he explains that eternal life is a gift from God and that it is found in his Son. This verse sums up the purpose of the whole letter: to give assurance to those who trust in Jesus.

For today: if you doubt your faith, do not rely only on your emotions. Read the Word, remember what God promised in Christ, and rest in that. You can say to God today: "Thank you, because your promise is firm."
exp.0:5:
It says that we cannot claim to be united with God (to have fellowship with him) and at the same time live in darkness, that is, in sin and deception. If we do, we lie and do not practice the truth. The words "say" and "walk" refer to what we claim and how we live each day.

The author, traditionally identified as the apostle John, writes to believers so that their joy may be complete. He has just said that God is light and that in him there is no darkness at all. Therefore, whoever says they know him should reflect that light in their conduct. The next verse offers hope: if we walk in the light, the blood of Jesus cleanses us.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our lives match what we say we believe. If there is something hidden or contradictory, there is no need to pretend: we can bring it before God with sincerity, trusting that his forgiveness cleanses us and helps us walk in the light.
exp.2:0:
It says that the Father's love is so great that he calls us his children, and that this is real, not just a title. The word "Behold" means "look, consider." The phrase "what manner of love" means "what kind of love, what a great love." "Unto him" means "to him." Because the world does not know God, it also does not understand those who belong to him.

It is part of the first letter of John, traditionally attributed to the apostle John. He writes to believers to give them assurance in their faith and to encourage them to live in love and purity. The next verse connects this identity as children with the hope of seeing Christ and being like him.

For today: when you feel rejected or misunderstood for following Jesus, remember who you are. Before thinking about what you do, begin the day by saying: "I am a child of God." From there, live with peace and simplicity.
exp.2:11:
This verse urges us not to be like Cain, who was of the evil one, meaning he acted under the influence of evil. Cain killed his brother Abel. John gives the reason: Cain's works were evil, and Abel's were righteous.

John, one of Jesus' apostles, writes to believers to teach them how the children of God are recognized: they live righteously and love one another. He uses Cain as the opposite example. Then he warns them that the world may hate them.

Today, when you feel envy or resentment toward someone who does good, do not let it grow. Ask God to change your heart, and seek to bless that person with a kind word or a practical help.
exp.2:6:
It says that no one should deceive us on this point: whoever practices righteousness is righteous, just as Jesus is righteous. The term "little children" is an affectionate way of addressing believers. The phrase "let no man deceive you" means "that no one should confuse them." "Doeth righteousness" means living in an upright way, consistently.

The apostle John, already elderly, writes like a shepherd who cares for his people. There were probably false teachers who claimed that one could know God without changing the way one lives. John answers that true faith shows itself in a life that resembles Christ. The verses that follow show the contrast with sin. Some scholars debate how to understand the phrase about not sinning, but all see here a call to a transformed life.

Today, it is not enough to say that we believe. We can ask God for help to obey him in something concrete this week, such as being honest at work or treating someone in our family better.
exp.3:3:
This verse says that believers belong to God. "Little children" is an affectionate way of speaking, the way a loving parent or pastor addresses those he cares for. The words "have overcome them" refer to the false teachers who deny that Jesus came as a real human being. The reason given is that God, who lives in believers, is more powerful than the evil at work in the world.

The speaker is the apostle John, according to Christian tradition, and he writes as a shepherd caring for his children in the faith. His readers were facing teachers who denied that Jesus had a real body. John wants them to test what they hear and not to be afraid.

For today: when a teaching confuses you or you feel pressure, compare it with what Christ said and did. Then rest in the truth that God is with you and is stronger than any fear.
exp.3:14:
This verse says that whoever openly declares that Jesus is the Son of God lives in a real union with God: God remains in that person, and that person in God. The word "whosoever" in the verse above is the one that covers everyone who makes this confession, so no separate explanation of it is needed here.

The writer is John, an apostle who knew Jesus, and he addresses believers who were facing false teachings about who Jesus was. That is why he insists that he and other witnesses saw the Son sent by the Father as the Savior of the world. To confess Jesus here is not just to repeat words, but to believe from the heart, and the context ties it to love.

For today: you do not need to be perfect to live close to God. Acknowledge Jesus sincerely, in prayer and before others, and let his love show in how you treat the people around you.
exp.4:8:
This verse compares two kinds of testimony. In everyday life we accept what people say: a judge believes witnesses, and we believe what others tell us. So much more should we believe God, whose testimony is greater, because He does not make mistakes or lie. And what God has declared is that Jesus is His Son.

The apostle John, already an old man, is writing to Christians who faced doubts and false teachings about who Jesus is. A note of honesty: the earlier passage about "three in heaven" does not appear in the oldest Greek manuscripts, and many scholars believe it was added later. The message of this verse stands just the same.

If we trust the word of fallible people, how much more should we trust the word of God? Today, when you doubt, lean on what God says about Jesus in His Word, not on your feelings.
exp.1:17:
John calls his readers "little children" with affection. He says it is already "the last time," that is, the final stage before Christ returns. They had heard that "the antichrist" would come, an opponent of Christ. But John says that there are already "many antichrists," people who oppose the truth about Jesus. That is how he knows what time they are living in.

John, an apostle and elder pastor, writes to Christians who were confused by teachers who had left the church and denied truths about Jesus. Earlier he spoke about not loving the world, which passes away. Christians ask how to understand "the last time"; some see it as the whole period between the first and second coming of Christ.

Today we can stand firm without fear or excessive curiosity about dates. Compare what you hear with what Jesus taught in the Bible, and live each day doing the will of God.
exp.4:9:
He who believes in the Son of God has the testimony within himself, that is, an inner assurance that it is true. On the other hand, whoever does not believe God treats him as a liar, because he rejects what God himself has declared about his Son.

The apostle John, according to Christian tradition, speaks to believers who needed assurance in the face of confusing teachings. He has just said that if we accept human testimony, God's testimony is even greater. Next he explains that testimony: God gave us eternal life, and that life is in his Son.

For today: when you doubt your faith, do not rely only on your feelings. Return to what God has said about Jesus in his Word, and ask him to strengthen your trust in him.
exp.1:13:
John repeats what he said before, now in the tone of "I have written." To the fathers, the mature believers, he reminds them that they know Christ, the one who is from the beginning, that is, the eternal one. To the young men, he tells them they are strong because the word of God abides in them, and for that reason they have overcome the wicked one, who is the devil.

The apostle John writes to believers at different stages of faith to give them assurance. Some think that "fathers," "young men," and "little children" describe spiritual maturity, while others think they are age groups. What follows (not loving the world) shows that he wants to encourage them before he warns them.

For today: spiritual strength does not come from our own willpower, but from letting the word dwell in us. Read the Bible every day, keep a verse in your heart, and use it when temptation comes.
exp.1:26:
The explanation says that believers have received from Christ an "anointing," that is, the Holy Spirit, who dwells in them. That is why they do not need anyone to teach them the basics of the truth, because that anointing teaches them, it is true, and it does not deceive. "You will remain in him" means they will stay firm in Christ.

The apostle John writes to believers who faced false teachers, those who "deceive you." These teachers denied truths about Jesus. John does not say that teaching is useless, since he himself is writing to them. His point is that they already have the essential truth of the gospel, and the Spirit helps them recognize it. Some understand the anointing as the Spirit, others as the message received; many see both together.

Today, when you hear a new teaching, compare it with what Jesus taught in the Bible and ask the Spirit to give you discernment. Keep learning with humility, but remain firm in Christ.
exp.2:4:
This verse says that Jesus came into the world with a clear purpose: to take away our sins. "Was manifested" means that he made himself visible, that he came as a person. It adds that in him there is no sin, that is, he is completely pure, and for that reason he can free us from sin.

The apostle John writes to believers who were facing false teachings. He has just said that sin is breaking God's law. Now he reminds them of something they already know: Christ came to take away sin, not to make it normal. Therefore, whoever lives united to him should not live in a constant practice of sin. Some scholars explain "take away" as bearing the punishment, others as removing its power; both ideas fit.

For today: when you feel tempted to downplay some sin, remember that Jesus came to take it away. Confess it sincerely and ask him for help to live differently.
exp.2:14:
It says that whoever hates his brother, that is, another believer, is already like a murderer in the eyes of God. And that such a person does not have eternal life abiding in him, meaning living and remaining in his heart. To hate is to hold a deep bitterness, a desire that the other person were no longer there.

The apostle John writes to believers who faced rejection from the world. He reminds them that the sign of having passed from death to life is love between brothers and sisters. Just before this verse he mentions Cain, who killed his brother. John shows that hatred is the root of that act, even when it does not reach violence.

For today: if you hold resentment against someone in your church or family, bring it to God in prayer and take a concrete step toward reconciliation, such as a phone call or a sincere apology.
exp.3:13:
This verse says that the Father sent his Son, Jesus, with a purpose: to be the Savior of the whole world. The speakers say they have seen him, that is, they were direct witnesses, and that they bear witness to him, meaning they tell it openly to others. The sending itself shows that it was the Father who took the initiative.

The writer is the apostle John, according to Christian tradition, addressing believers. He has just said that no one has seen God at any time, but that his love becomes visible when believers love one another. Here he points to the greatest proof of that love: Jesus, whom the apostles did see. He goes on to speak of confessing Jesus and of living in love.

For today: if God sent his Son out of love for the world, we can simply tell what Jesus has done in our lives, and treat those near us with that same love.
exp.3:4:
This verse says that the false teachers John has been talking about belong to the world. That is why what they teach sounds the way the world thinks, and worldly people listen to them gladly. "World" here does not mean creation, but the system of ideas and values that lives turned away from God.

John, already old, writes like a shepherd caring for his little children. Some false prophets denied that Jesus Christ had come in the flesh, and John wants believers not to be frightened or deceived. He reminds them that the God who is in them is greater than the world.

For today: do not measure a teaching by its popularity. That many applaud it does not prove it is true. Compare it with what Jesus taught, and ask God for wisdom to discern.
exp.3:10:
This verse says that, since God loved us in such a great way, we too have the obligation, the heartfelt duty, to love one another. "Beloved" means dear ones, people whom God loves. The message is simple: the love we receive from God does not stay with us, but must flow out to others.

The writer is the apostle John, in a letter addressed to Christians. Just before, he explains that God showed his love by sending his Son Jesus to take away the weight of our sins. John wants his readers to see that loving others comes from first knowing God's love. He then adds that when we love one another, God's love becomes visible among us.

Today we can think of a person who is hard to get along with and show them a concrete act of love: listen to them with patience, forgive them, or help them, remembering how much God has forgiven and cared for us.
exp.3:12:
This verse says that we can know with certainty that we live united with God, and that He lives in us, because He has given us of His Spirit. "We know" means "we know for sure." "We are in him" speaks of a close relationship with God. The Holy Spirit is the sign of that union.

John, one of Jesus' apostles, writes to believers to encourage them and give them assurance. Earlier he spoke about love: if God loved us, we ought to love one another. No one has seen God, but His presence is evident when His love acts in His people. Then John adds that confessing Jesus as the Son of God confirms that union.

For today: if you doubt your relationship with God, do not rely only on your feelings. Look for faith in Jesus and a desire to love others within you. Ask the Spirit to help you forgive or serve someone this week.
exp.2:16:
This verse asks: if someone has what is needed to live, sees a brother in need, and feels no compassion for him, how can he claim that the love of God is in his life? The words "goods of this world" refer to material resources, such as money, food, or clothing. Shutting up one's compassion means hardening the heart and refusing to feel pity. "Brother" here refers to a fellow believer.

The apostle John is writing to Christians to show them how true love is recognized. He has just spoken about Jesus, who gave his life for us. Now he brings that love down to everyday life: if we should be willing to give up our lives, we can at least share what we have.

Today, think of someone close to you who is going through a specific need, and ask God what you can give or do for them this week. A simple gesture counts.
exp.1:28:
This verse says that if you know that God is righteous, then you can be sure that everyone who does what is right has been born of him. "Doeth righteousness" means living in an upright way, doing what is right before God. "Born of him" refers to being a child of God, having received new spiritual life.

The apostle John, now an older man, speaks to believers whom he calls "little children." He writes to encourage them to remain firm in Christ and to have confidence when he returns. He also wants to help them tell true faith apart from false teachings. John presents a righteous life as a sign that someone belongs to God, not as a way of earning his love.

For today: ask yourself honestly whether your daily choices, at home, at work, and in your words, reflect the character of your Father. Ask God for his help, without anxiety, to live as his child.
exp.4:18:
We are told that believers can have assurance that they belong to God. The verse also says that the whole world "lieth in wickedness." This phrase can be understood as "lies under the power of the evil one," that is, under his influence. Other translations express it this way.

The apostle John, already elderly according to tradition, writes to believers who were facing false teachings. He wants to give them certainty and steadiness. He contrasts those who are of God with a world far from him. Some debate whether "the world" refers to people or to the system that opposes God, but in either case the contrast is clear.

Today we can live with humility and hope. We should not be frightened or settle into the wickedness around us. Belonging to God invites us to be light, to love through actions, and to ask him to keep us.
exp.3:16:
It says that God's love reaches its goal or maturity when it lives in us, and so we can be at peace before the day of judgment. "Made perfect" here means complete, brought to its fullness. The reason is that "as he is, so are we in this world": Christ is loved by the Father, and we, united to him, are loved as well.

John, the apostle, writes to believers to give them assurance. He has just spoken of God being love and of whoever confesses Jesus abiding in God. Then he will say that perfect love casts out fear. Some think that "the day of judgment" refers to the final judgment; the text gives no further detail.

Today, if fear weighs on you that you are not enough for God, remember that he loved you first. Pray calmly, and let his love, not your performance, be the foundation of your confidence.
exp.1:9:
It says that whoever truly loves their brother lives in the light, that is, in the way of living that pleases God. Here "brother" refers above all to a fellow believer. The phrase about there being no stumbling in him can be understood in two ways: that this person does not stumble or fall, or that he is not a cause of stumbling for others. Both ideas fit the text.

The apostle John, already elderly according to Christian tradition, writes to believers to give them assurance. He reminds them of the command to love one another, which Jesus taught. John insists that saying "I am in the light" is not enough if there is hatred in the heart.

Today, we can examine whether we hold a grudge against someone in our church, family, or workplace. Let us ask God for help to forgive and take a concrete step: greeting them, listening, or making peace.
exp.1:25:
John says that what he has just written has a specific purpose: to warn believers about those who want to deceive them. The words "I have written this to you" refer to what he said earlier about remaining in what they heard from the beginning. The word "deceive" means to lead someone away from the truth by making them believe something false.

The one speaking is the apostle John, who writes like an elderly shepherd to his "little children" in the faith. In those communities there were teachers who denied that Jesus is the Son of God and who turned others away from the original teaching. John wants the believers to stay firm and secure.

For today: before accepting a teaching, compare it with what Jesus and the apostles taught, as it is recorded in the Bible. Make time to read the Scriptures and to pray, so that your faith does not depend only on what others say.
exp.0:4:
This verse says that the central message the apostles heard from Jesus is that God is light. The phrase "no darkness at all" means that nothing dark is found in God: no wickedness, no lying, no deceit. He is completely pure, true, and good.

The one speaking is the author of the letter, traditionally identified as the apostle John, although the text does not give his name. He speaks as a witness to what he saw and heard from Jesus. He writes so that believers may have fellowship with God and with one another, and so that their joy may be complete. The verses that follow show that, because God is light, anyone who says they know him must live in line with that.

Today we can live with sincerity before God. If something in your life is hidden, bring it into the light in prayer. His light not only reveals sin, it also offers forgiveness through the blood of Jesus.
exp.3:15:
This verse says that believers have come to know and to trust the love God has for them. It then states that "God is love": love is not only something God does, but part of who He is. Whoever lives in love remains united to God, and God remains in that person. Here "lives" means "remains" or "dwells."

The writer is the apostle John, according to Christian tradition, addressing believers. Earlier he spoke of having seen Jesus and of the Father sending the Son as Savior of the world. Afterward he explains that this love takes away the fear of judgment. His purpose is to give assurance and to show that true faith is seen in love.

Today, when you doubt that God loves you, remember what Christ did for you. Then take one concrete step of love: forgive, help, or listen to someone this week.
exp.3:5:
John says that "we," meaning the apostles who taught the message of Christ, are from God. Whoever truly knows God receives that teaching, and whoever is not from God does not receive it. In this way the spirit of truth is told apart from the spirit of error. The words "hear" and "know" here mean receiving and accepting, not merely listening.

John, already an elderly man, writes to believers who were troubled by false teachers who denied that Jesus came as a true human being (verses 1-3). He wants to give them assurance: they belong to God and can recognize what is faithful to the apostles' teaching.

For today: before accepting a teaching, compare it with what Christ and the apostles left us in the Bible. Do this with humility and with love, as John asks right after, without looking down on anyone.
exp.3:19:
This verse says it is false to claim that we love God if at the same time we hate our brother. The word "hateth" in the verse means to hate or to treat with contempt. John reasons from what is visible to what is invisible: if we cannot love a person we can see, it is hard to believe that we love God, whom we cannot see.

The writer is the apostle John, according to Christian tradition. He writes to believers to encourage them to live in love. Shortly before, he spoke of God's love that reached us first. So love for others is the sign that this love has truly changed us.

Today we can ask ourselves: is there someone I hold a grudge against? Let us ask God for help to forgive, and take one concrete step: greet that person, listen, ask forgiveness, or do them a favor.
exp.0:7:
This verse says that if we claim we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. The word "sin" here refers to our condition and to our real failings.

The writer is John, the apostle, according to the oldest Christian tradition. He writes to believers who were listening to false teachings. Some scholars think these were people who considered themselves free of guilt. John does not frighten them. He shows them that walking in the light includes recognizing our need for forgiveness, and that the blood of Jesus cleanses us.

Today, instead of making excuses or hiding your mistakes, bring them honestly before God. He already knows you, and his arms are open to forgive you.
exp.3:11:
The explanation says that no one has ever seen God with their eyes. But when we love one another, God lives in us. His love comes to be "complete" in us, that is, it reaches its goal and is shown in full in our lives. The word "perfect" in the verse means it reaches its goal and is shown in full in our lives.

The speaker is John the apostle, according to Christian tradition, writing to believers. He has just said that God loved us first and sent his Son because of our sins. For this reason, loving one another is the natural response. Moreover, John insists that love for God is not just an idea: it becomes visible in how we treat our brothers and sisters.

Today, we can show God's love through a concrete act: forgiving someone, visiting a sick person, or helping someone who needs it. Although people cannot see God, they can see his love in us.
exp.2:23:
This verse says that whoever obeys God's commandments lives united with Him, and God lives united with that person. And the proof that God remains in us is the Holy Spirit whom He has given us. Note that the text says the words for "in him" in an old style of writing; it is understood as "and God in that person."

Here the apostle John speaks, writing to believers to give them assurance. Just before, he said what the central commandment is: to believe in Jesus Christ and to love one another. So "keeping his commandments" points above all to trusting in Jesus and loving others.

For today: if you doubt your faith, do not look only at your feelings. Look at whether you trust in Christ and whether you try to love those around you, and remember that God's Spirit in you is the sign that He remains with you.
exp.3:8:
This verse says that God showed his love for us in a concrete way: he sent his only Son into the world so that we might have life through him. The word "only begotten" means one of a kind, the Son who is loved in a special way. The phrase "live through him" speaks of a true life that comes from Jesus.

The author is John, who writes to believers, according to Christian tradition. He stresses that loving one another is a sign of knowing God. Just before this verse he says that God is love. Here he explains where that love can be seen: in the sending of Jesus. He then adds that Jesus came as the one who takes away our sins, a sacrifice that covers them.

For today: when you doubt that God loves you, look to Jesus, not only to your circumstances. And let that love you have received move you to treat someone close to you with patience and generosity this week.
exp.1:21:
It says that the true liar is the one who denies that Jesus is the Christ, that is, the Messiah promised by God. John calls such a person "antichrist," someone who opposes Christ. He adds that whoever rejects the Son also rejects the Father, because the two are united.

The writer is the apostle John, according to Christian tradition. He addresses believers who were troubled by people who had left the community and were teaching false things about Jesus. John does not want to frighten them, but to remind them that they already know the truth through the anointing they received from the Holy One, which many understand as the work of the Holy Spirit.

Today we can examine what we hear about Jesus without being carried away only by what sounds good. It is wise to return to what God has shown us in his Word and to remain firm in it, trusting in Christ as Lord and Savior.
exp.0:3:
The explanation says that the apostles write this letter with a purpose: that the joy of believers may be full, that is, complete, lacking nothing. Some ancient manuscripts say "our joy" instead of "your joy," and scholars debate which reading is original. Both ideas fit together: the joy of all grows together.

The one speaking is John, along with the witnesses who knew Jesus. He has just said that they saw and heard the eternal Life, and he wants others to share that fellowship with the Father and the Son. His joy comes from seeing others united with God.

For today: the deepest joy does not come from circumstances, but from being close to God and to other believers. This week, read the Bible with someone else and share together what God shows you.
exp.3:2:
It says that every spirit or message that does not acknowledge that Jesus Christ truly came as a human being, "in the flesh," does not come from God. John calls it the spirit of the antichrist, that is, one that opposes Christ. The believers had already heard that this would come, and John affirms that it was already at work.

The apostle John writes to believers who were facing false teachers. Many think they denied the real humanity of Jesus, though scholars describe these ideas in different ways. John wants his readers to test what they hear and not be deceived. Then he encourages them: the Spirit who lives in them is greater than the one who is in the world.

Today, before accepting a teaching, compare it with what the Bible says about Jesus: God made man, who lived, died, and rose again for us. Do not be carried away just by what sounds spiritual or convincing.
exp.0:9:
If we say, "I have never sinned," we are calling God a liar. And his word, which is his message and his truth, does not live within us.

John, one of Jesus' apostles, writes to believers. As we understand it, he wants to help them live in God's light and not deceive themselves. Earlier he spoke of denying sin as a self-deception. Here he goes further: denying it contradicts what God has already said about us. But the verse before offers hope: God forgives those who confess.

Today we can pray with sincerity, without excuses, and tell God where we have failed. If needed, we can also ask forgiveness from the person we have hurt. God receives us with grace.
exp.1:27:
John calls the believers "little children" with affection and asks them to "abide" in Christ, that is, to remain united with him and not drift away. So when he "appears" (is revealed, returns), they will have "confidence" (boldness, peace of mind) and will not be "ashamed" (put to shame) before him at his coming.

The apostle John, now an elderly man, speaks to Christians who were facing teachers who were deceiving them. He reminds them that the Spirit, who anoints them, guides them into the truth. For that reason he encourages them to stay firm in what they have already learned about Christ.

For today: faith is not only a beginning but a daily journey. Seek Christ every day in prayer and in his Word, and obey him in the simple things. In this way you can await his return with peace and not with fear.
exp.3:17:
It says that where there is true love, there is no fear. Complete love drives fear out of the heart, because fear brings punishment, that is, torment. Someone who lives in fear of God, expecting to be punished, has not yet fully understood the love of God.

The apostle John is writing to believers. He has just said that God is love and that we can have confidence on the day of judgment. Here he is speaking of the fear of being condemned. Some understand it to mean the dread of final punishment, not reverent respect for God.

Today, if you are afraid of not being accepted by God, remember that he loved you first. Speak to him with confidence, and let his love, not fear, guide how you treat others.
exp.1:2:
This verse says that we can know whether we truly know God by a specific sign: whether we keep his commandments. "Knowing" here is not just knowing facts about God, but having a relationship with him. "Keeping" means obeying and living according to what he commands.

The one speaking is John, the apostle, traditionally recognized as the author of this letter. He writes to believers whom he calls "my little children." He has just said that Jesus forgives our sins, and now he makes clear that this forgiveness is no excuse for living as if nothing mattered. He also wants them to be sure of their faith and not to be deceived by those who only talk.

Today, instead of asking ourselves only "How do I feel about God?", we can ask "How am I living?" Choose one command of Jesus today, such as forgiving or loving someone difficult, and practice it. If you fail, remember that we have an advocate before the Father.
exp.2:17:
John calls his readers "little children," speaking with the affection of a shepherd. He asks that love not stay in mere words or empty talk, but show itself in actions and in sincerity. Loving truly costs something, and people can see it.

The apostle John writes to believers who already know the love of Christ, who gave his life for us. Just before this, he speaks of someone who has possessions, sees his brother in need, and shuts his heart against him, that is, hardens his compassion. John says that the love of God does not look like that. He then adds that practical love gives us confidence before God.

Today, think of someone close to you who is going through a hard time: food, transportation, company, or help with a bill. Instead of only saying "I am praying for you," do something concrete and possible this week, and pray as well.
exp.3:1:
This verse gives a way to recognize whether a teaching comes from God: every spirit, that is, every message or teacher, that confesses (openly declares) that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh (came as a true human being) is of God. The word "know" here means "recognize" or "discern."

John, the apostle, writes to believers who were surrounded by false teachers. Some denied that Jesus was truly God become man. That is why John asks his readers to test the spirits and not to believe everything they hear. Scholars do not agree on exactly which group this was, so it is wise not to claim more than the text says.

For today: before accepting a teaching, compare it with the Bible and ask what it says about Jesus. If it teaches that He is God and came as a true man, you are on the right path. If it denies this or waters it down, be wary, with humility.
exp.1:19:
They have an anointing from the Holy One, that is, from Christ or from God, and by it they "know all things." The anointing is a picture of being set apart and equipped by God; many understand it to be the Holy Spirit. "All things" does not mean knowing everything, but knowing the essential truth about Jesus, as the next verse shows.

John writes as an aged pastor to his dear children in the faith. Some teachers had left the church and denied that Jesus is the Christ. John wants believers not to be frightened or doubtful, and he reminds them of what God has already given them.

For today: if you have trusted in Jesus, do not live in fear before confusing teachings. Compare what you hear with what Christ teaches in the Bible, and ask God to give you discernment.
exp.2:18:
This verse says that when we love with actions and not only with words, we have a sign that we belong to the truth. That sign also settles our hearts before God. "Assure" means to make certain or to set at rest: our conscience rests in the presence of God.

The one writing is John, the aged apostle, who speaks affectionately to his "little children." He has just asked them to help the brother in need, because closing the heart to someone's need contradicts the love of God. The verses that follow explain that if our heart condemns us, God is greater and knows all things. Some understand this to bring comfort; others, to bring sobriety.

For today: look for a specific need close to you, such as that of a family member, a neighbor, or someone in your church, and help that person this week with a simple act. Let your love be seen in deeds.
exp.1:20:
John tells his readers that he has not written to them because they do not know the truth, but because they do know it. He also reminds them of a clear principle: no lie comes from the truth. The phrase "as to those who know it" simply means "as to those who know it" in the sense of those who are acquainted with it. Truth and falsehood do not mix, nor do they have the same origin.

The apostle John writes to anxious believers because some who had once been among them had left and were teaching errors about Jesus. John does not want to frighten them but to give them assurance. He reminds them that they have the anointing from the Holy One, which many understand to be the Holy Spirit, though some connect it with the teaching they received. With this they can tell what is true from what is false.

Today, you do not have to live in fear amid so many voices and opinions. Know Jesus well through the Bible, ask the Holy Spirit to guide you, and compare every teaching with what Christ really said and did.
exp.4:3:
Says that everyone who has been born of God overcomes the world. And the victory that overcomes the world is our faith. "Whatsoever is born" refers to everyone who has been born again spiritually by God. "The world" here does not mean creation, but the system of thinking and desires that opposes God.

The apostle John writes this, according to Christian tradition, to believers who needed assurance. He had been speaking about love for God and obeying him, and he clarifies that his commandments are not burdensome. Then he explains that faith in Jesus, the Son of God, is what gives the victory. Some scholars think he was also responding to false teachings about Jesus.

For today: when you feel pressure to live as if God did not matter, do not trust only your own strength. Trust in Jesus, pray, and take one concrete step of obedience, even a small one. That simple faith is what sustains you.
exp.1:11:
John calls his readers "little children," a tender, fatherly way of speaking to believers he loves. He writes to them because their sins have already been forgiven for the sake of Jesus' name. This means the forgiveness comes through Jesus, through who He is and what He did on the cross.

The apostle John, already elderly according to tradition, writes to several churches. Earlier he spoke about loving one's brother and walking in the light. Now he reminds them that their security does not depend on how well they perform, but on the fact that Christ has forgiven them. Then he addresses fathers and young men, and some think he is referring to different stages of faith, though not everyone agrees.

For today: if guilt weighs on you, remember that your forgiveness rests on the name of Jesus. Confess your failures to Him and walk in freedom, loving others as He loved you.
exp.1:12:
This verse speaks to three groups: fathers, young men, and little children (the newest in the faith). It tells the fathers that they know Christ, the one who is from the beginning, meaning the one who existed before all things. It reminds the young men that they have overcome the wicked one, that is, the devil. It tells the little children that they know the Father.

The speaker is John the apostle, already an old man according to Christian tradition. He is writing to believers who were facing false teachers. He wants to give them assurance: their faith is real. Some think the three groups describe stages of spiritual growth, and others think they describe physical ages; the text allows for both readings.
